AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE
AbstractText.content: To compare cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors of black and non-black children participating in Project Healthy Schools (PHS), a school-based wellness program.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: Participants were surveyed and participated in physiological screenings pre- and post-PHS intervention.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Middle schools in 4 Michigan communities of varying socioeconomic status.

AbstractText.Label: PARTICIPANTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 3813 sixth-grade students comprised the survey sample, and 2297 sixth-grade students comprised the screening sample.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTION
AbstractText.content: Project Healthy Schools is a school-based intervention designed to reduce the risk of obesity and CVD in children through the promotion of healthy eating and physical activity.

AbstractText.Label: MEASURES
AbstractText.content: Physical examination, blood test, and self-reported survey data on dietary habits, physical activity, and sedentary behaviors were collected pre- and post-PHS.

AbstractText.Label: ANALYSIS
AbstractText.content: Paired and independent t tests were used for physiologic variables. Wilcoxon sign-rank and rank-sum tests were used for survey variables.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: At baseline, blacks had a higher percentage of overweight/obese students (43% vs 34%; P < .0001) and demonstrated poorer health habits than non-blacks; however, non-blacks had poorer lipid profiles. At follow-up (post-PHS intervention), both groups demonstrated significant improvements in physiological measures and health behaviors.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Despite disparities between the groups at both baseline and follow-up, changes seen post-PHS intervention were beneficial in both groups. These results suggest that early intervention for risk factor modification is possible and may be of great importance in the prevention of CVD, particularly in high-risk groups.
